title: Vedanta (revisited)
hook: a thin new moon, a tree branch, and the Brahma Sutra's second line: you can point at what you can't hold

segments.voice: Yesterday Vedanta opened its book with a wish: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. What question did you find yourself holding? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.
screen: `THE WISH TO KNOW.` · `THEN WHAT IS IT?`

segments.voice: It's dusk, and a parent is crouched beside a small child, pointing at the sky. The new moon is up, a thin curve, almost nothing. The child can't find it. So the parent tries again. See that tree? See the top branch? Right above it. And suddenly the child sees. Nobody thinks the moon is sitting on the branch. The branch was only a way of getting the eyes to the right place. Vedanta teachers have a name for this move. They call it the branch-and-moon way. Today it explains the second line of the Brahma Sutra, the one that tries to say what Brahman is.
screen: `A THIN NEW MOON.` → `SEE THAT BRANCH?` → `THE BRANCH ONLY POINTS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Sutra said it wanted to know Brahman. So the obvious next question is: what is Brahman? The second line answers, but not the way you might expect. It says, in effect: that from which the birth and so on of this world come. Birth, staying, and dissolving. Brahman is that from which all of it arises, by which it lasts, into which it goes. That's a branch, not a moon. It doesn't describe Brahman. It points from things you know, a world being born and fading, toward their source. The line leans on the Taittiriya Upanishad, where a father gives his son nearly the same pointer: seek that from which these beings are born. We followed that son, Bhrigu, in an earlier year. Here it becomes a definition. Vedanta teachers say there are two ways to say what something is. One is by a mark that belongs to the thing itself. The other is by a mark that only points, like the branch. The Taittiriya gives the first kind too, in another line: Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite. But even there, some readers, Shankara among them, hear pointing. Truth, so not false. Knowledge, so not dull matter. Infinite, so not this one thing or that one. When a tradition points instead of describing, it isn't being vague. It's being careful. Some things you reach by following a gesture, not by holding a picture.
screen: `THAT FROM WHICH THE WORLD ARISES.` · `A POINTER, NOT A PORTRAIT.` · `TRUTH, KNOWLEDGE, THE INFINITE.` · `CAREFUL, NOT VAGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow a pointer. Settle and notice one breath arriving. Ask, without words if you can, where it comes from. Then notice it staying for a moment. Then notice it leaving, and ask where it goes. Don't try to picture an answer. Let the breath be the branch, and let your attention rest just past it, in the quiet it rises from and returns to. If a picture shows up, let it go, and return to the next breath. If you pray, you can let the breath carry a name you hold dear. The bell holds the time.
Vedanta. Today, its way of pointing: Brahman as that from which the world is born, by which it lasts, into which it returns. Today's word.
Your line: Vedanta, revisited. Today, pick one thing you use or eat and ask where it came from, then where that came from, a few steps back. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: In traditional Vedanta study, teachers explain the Brahma Sutra's second line alongside Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1 and 2.1, and they often use the image of showing the moon through a tree branch to explain how a definition can point rather than describe.

fork.setup: a child can't find a thin new moon in the dusk. what do you do?
options: point to a branch just below it.
tell the child to wait for a full moon.
fork.reveal: the branch gets the eyes there. Vedanta teachers use this to explain the Sutra's second line.

original.note: Sanskrit: Brahma Sutra 1.1.2, roughly: that from which the birth and so on of this come.

trapdoor: what you thought: Vedanta gives a description of God.
what it means: the Brahma Sutra points at Brahman as that from which the world arises, lasts and returns, like a branch pointing at the moon.
what a scholar hears: Brahma Sutra 1.1.2, janmadyasya yatah, read with Taittiriya 3.1 and 2.1, and the distinction between a defining mark of the thing itself and a mark that only points.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 1.1.2 (that from which the origin and so on of this world come)
Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1 (that from which these beings are born, by which they live, into which they enter)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1 (Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite)

notes: The branch-and-moon method (shakha-chandra nyaya) is a traditional Vedanta illustration; confirm it is fairly applied to Brahma Sutra 1.1.2.
The two kinds of definition are svarupa-lakshana and tatastha-lakshana; the script avoids the Sanskrit terms and their etymology. Confirm the framing.
'Some readers, Shankara among them, hear pointing' in satyam jnanam anantam (truth as not-false, etc.) follows Shankara's commentary on Taittiriya 2.1; confirm.
Bhrigu's story (Taittiriya 3) was told in year two; this day only refers back to it.
